chapter_theme: Fragments preserved in the Purattirattu on the madness of love, the dangers and fleetingness of wealth, killing and truth, the late turn to renunciation and the futility of trying to escape karma while still attached; their order is the editor's and no story can be rebuilt from them.

cast.role: an unnamed first-person or arguing voice in a fragment; the verse does not say who speaks

24.reading: When the sickness of love takes deep root, men ride the palm-stem calling it a horse in every public square, put on erukku clusters, and stand like the possessed while others jeer.
24.nuance: The verse reworks Kuruntokai 17 almost phrase for phrase (மா என... மடல் ஏறுப, எருக்கு, ஆர்ப்ப, காழ்க்கொள்), but recasts the lover's own boast as a symptom: it adds புன்மை (baseness), பேய் (possession) and நோய் (disease). Line 2 is damaged (see source_issues).

claims.claim: love grown deep-rooted drives a man to base public folly

25.reading: Lovesick men laugh till their sides split, feel shame and then want none, lie where they have crept in, live on dreams and fancies, forget food, weep and cannot sleep; desire for a woman's fine shoulders makes a suffering the whole country knows.
25.nuance: A catalogue of symptoms in the manner of the akam books, but told from outside and without sympathy; the last line's நாடறி துன்பம் turns private longing into public talk (alar).

26.reading: Those who befriend kings live off their realm and those who befriend snakes make them dance for a living, but of women with bangled forearms the ancients said no art avails, and let them go.
26.nuance: The sense of விரகிலர் (no art, no means) and the subject of விடுத்தனர் are not certain; the verse may instead mean the women themselves are without guile. This is the fragment's view of women, one of several in the chapter (46, 47).

claims.claim: women cannot be managed by skill as kings and snakes can, so the wise renounce them

27.reading: Those who carry off by stealth many goods from others' houses reap this fruit: they are gathered, held fast by hand and foot, and cut so they cannot run.
27.nuance: The punishment is presented as the theft's own பயன் (fruit), in this life; the verse does not name the king, only the seizing and cutting.

claims.claim: the fruit of theft is mutilation at the king's hands

28.reading: Give up lying, take on truthfulness and walk the path of dharma without doubt: those who do are seen to reach a world without daily pain or reproach.
28.nuance: Truth here is a companion of dharma, worn like an ornament (பூண்டு), not the whole of it; கண்டதே ('this is what has been seen') rests the promise on observation.

claims.claim: truthfulness together with dharma wins a world free of pain

29.reading: Lack of learning, loss of wealth in hand, affliction and being drawn into lie after lie surely follow from something the verse calls only 'that'; forbid it and guard yourselves.
29.nuance: அது in line 4 has no antecedent in the verse: the vice was named in a lost context (drink or gambling would fit the list, but the verse does not say). Line 2's நல்லில் செல்லல் is unclear.

claims.claim: a certain vice brings ignorance, poverty, affliction and habitual lying

30.reading: If you want lasting fame that lights the world, and fear the boundless pain of reeling among the four states of birth, give up deceitful killing that terrifies living beings: so the knowing have said.
30.nuance: கதி நான்கு, the four states (gods, humans, beasts, hell), is the Jain reckoning of births; the verse rests its rule on the authority of அறிந்தார் rather than stating it in its own voice.

claims.claim: killing living beings binds one to wander among the four states of birth

31.reading: Wealth slips from the hand and departs by flood, by negligence, by mighty kings, by fire, by kinsmen's claims and by thieves; those who give up the wealth in their house without clinging to it pass beyond the scorned grief of great suffering.
31.nuance: The six thieves of wealth (flood, forgetfulness, kings, fire, heirs, robbers) are a list; the last line could also be read as saying those who cling suffer more, so the verse's direction is not fixed.

claims.claim: wealth is lost in many ways, and those who let it go without clinging escape its grief

32.reading: Those who let go of the borrowed wealth that perishes and passes to others, and who did not seek even a little of it, the verse appears to say, are free of great suffering.
32.nuance: வம்பப் பொருள் ('wealth that is a stranger's', borrowed) is the key image; line 1 and the close of line 4 do not yield a sure sense.

claims.claim: those who renounce fleeting wealth escape great suffering

33.reading: Poverty is disgrace and possession is fear for one's life; wealth lasts little, deludes much and brings baseness, so the renunciation of those who never went near it is excellent.

claims.claim: both lacking and having wealth bring harm, so renouncing it is best

34.reading: Wealth is hard to gather and easy to lose, gives little joy and much trembling, and is ignoble by nature; the strength of those who never wanted it is excellent.
34.nuance: A companion to 33 with the same closing frame (ஒழிந்தார் ... விழுமிதே), turning from renunciation (துறவு) to the strength (விறல்) it takes.

claims.claim: not desiring wealth at all is the true strength

35.reading: Without wealth there is no living, with it base men kill you and the taken die; whether one has it or not, it shows itself worthless for this life and the next and is nothing to hold.
35.nuance: Line 2's கொளப்பட்டும் வீடுவர் is compressed; it may mean the robbed die, or the rich are seized and killed.

claims.claim: wealth, had or lacked, is barren for this world and the next

36.reading: A speaker says that now the spear-eyed young women no longer desire him, the staff shows his road and killing Death is near; past forty, with grey hair come as messenger, he resolves to renounce, for youth does not last.
36.nuance: The motive is mixed: renunciation is chosen when desire has already left him (மடவார் விழைவு ஒழிய). யாம் may be a plural of dignity or a group; the fragment does not say who speaks.
36.event: An unnamed speaker, past forty and greying, resolves to renounce.

claims.claim: since youth does not last, renunciation should follow when age comes

37.reading: Youth does not last, pleasures do not stay, wealth is the same and floods of sorrow come daily; so for the state you will go to, always, like farmers who plough, sow and water, make your provision.

claims.claim: merit for the next birth must be cultivated continually, as a farmer tends his field

38.reading: For those set on cutting off birth, even the body is excess, so what further ties; while these remain, karma clings and the soul wanders among many wombs, hard to escape.
38.nuance: Lines 1-2 are Kural 345 almost word for word; lines 3-4 add the reason the couplet leaves unstated, a chain from attachment to karma to யோனிகள் (wombs).

claims.claim: as long as body and attachment remain, karma clings and drives the soul through many births

echoes.words: மற்றும் தொடர்ப்பா(டு) எவன்கொல் பிறப்(பு)அறுக்கல் உற்றார்க்(கு) உடம்பு மிகை

39.reading: Trying to drive off sin born of attachment while still standing in attachment is like washing a blood-stained cloth by dipping it in the same blood.

claims.claim: sin born of attachment cannot be removed while one keeps attachment

40.reading: A speaker laments: we gave no gifts and did no penance, but spent ourselves in moonlit groves; is there escape for us and the musk-haired one? The word of those whose creed has cast off pride is not false.
40.nuance: நானம் தோய்குழல் may be a vocative to a woman or the woman whose love distracted the speaker; the 'pride-free' ones (மானம்தீர் கொள்கையார்) are probably ascetics, whose warning the speaker now accepts.

claims.claim: without giving and austerity there is no escape from what follows

41.reading: The verse bids the hearers stop some heartfelt rejoicing (lines 1-2 are obscure) and closes on the saying that there is one mighty being in the world who removes fearful suffering.
41.nuance: Whether the closing saying is affirmed (a deliverer such as a Jina) or held up as a false comfort cannot be fixed from the fragment; என்னும் ஆறே suggests it is the second half of a comparison whose first half is unclear.

42.reading: Yoking oxen and ploughing hard yet expecting the green crop without seed is like the man without austerity toiling and suffering for wealth and pleasures.
42.nuance: Austerity is the seed, not the labour: effort without past merit grows nothing.

claims.claim: without the seed of austerity, toil for wealth and pleasure yields only suffering

43.reading: In the rich land the sweet sugarcane, rivalling the red paddy, rises in anger at the areca, and the areca, refusing to look, hides its face in the clouds.
43.nuance: A description of fertile country by rivalry of crops, the kind of country-praise that opens the long epics; nothing in the verse ties it to a place.

44.reading: Learning got from the family brings things to completion, wealth relieves the wasting hunger of struggling kin; is there any shame in crossing the long, ground-splitting wasteland to bring it back?
44.nuance: The voice is an arguer for going after wealth, as in the akam books' parting for wealth; the fragment does not say who argues, and its editor's order sets it among verses that condemn wealth (33-35).

claims.claim: seeking wealth across hard country is honourable because it feeds one's kin

45.reading: When a ruined man says 'this is my state' and seeks refuge, the many kin who were no true friends say what they please, scorn him and go stand where he cannot reach them.

claims.claim: kin desert and scorn one who is ruined

46.reading: Hoping to unite a woman's divided mind is like longing to gather back oil that has spread on clear water and gone in every direction.
46.nuance: The fragment's view of women; the simile is of something past recall, not merely difficult.

claims.claim: a woman's divided mind cannot be made single again

47.reading: Forcing love is like tearing open a long bud by hand; when care and affection are born, a woman, bewildered, embraces the man of herself.
47.nuance: Line 2 (a finely wrought doll standing hidden and listening) does not fit a sure syntax, and the verse may say instead that love comes by stealth, as one overhears from behind a screen.

links.note: The fragment takes over Kuruntokai 17's palm-horse, erukku garland, jeering street and heartwood-hard love, and adds baseness, possession and disease.
links.teaches: The same four acts that the Sangam lover names as love's compulsion, in his own voice, become in a renunciant work the symptoms of a sickness to be avoided: the change of speaker is what changes the verdict.

gains.a: the source of its catalogue, which shows that the 'disease' was once a lover's threat to win his woman
gains.b: an outsider's moral reading of its acts, which the lover's own speech never gives

links.note: Verse 5 says the knowing found no guard for women though food, wealth and learning can be guarded; verse 26 says no art manages them as kings and snakes are managed, so the wise let them go.
links.teaches: Read together, the two verses carry the claim from 'women cannot be kept' to its renunciant conclusion, 'so give them up'.

links.note: The fragment states that a thief's fruit is to be seized and cut; the Pandya tells Kannaki that killing a thief is no cruel sceptre, then finds he heeded a goldsmith and was himself the thief.
links.teaches: The rule that theft earns the king's punishment holds only when the thief is truly known; the epic shows the same rule, unexamined, turning the punisher into the criminal.

links.note: Kural 297 says unbroken truthfulness makes all other virtues unnecessary; verse 28 pairs giving up falsehood with practising dharma and promises a painless world for both.
links.teaches: Truth can be held as the whole of virtue or as one ornament worn with the rest; the fragment takes the second view and pays for it with a promise of the next world that the Kural does not make.

gains.a: the Kural's sharper claim, against which its pairing of truth and dharma shows as a choice
gains.b: a reward named for the truthful, where the couplet only ranks virtues

links.note: Both rest on what the knowing say (என்ப; கூறினர் அறிந்தார்): Kural 330 reasons from a wretched life back to killing; verse 30 names the four states of birth as killing's issue.
links.teaches: The fragment supplies the cosmology, the Jain four states of birth, that the couplet's backward inference from suffering to killing needs but never states.

gains.a: a statement of the harsh inference its rule implies: that the wretched now are killers before
gains.b: an explicit rebirth scheme in place of its bare 'they say'

links.note: Verse 33 says poverty is disgrace and wealth fear, so those who never approach wealth are best; verse 44 asks what shame there is in crossing the wasteland for wealth that feeds one's kin.
links.teaches: Set side by side by the anthology's editor, the two answer the same question opposite ways: whether the duty to feed kin makes the pursuit of wealth honourable or only another snare.

links.note: Both start from wealth that will not stay; Naladiyar 2 says share it at once, since it turns like a wheel, while verse 34 praises those who never wanted it.
links.teaches: The fleetingness of wealth supports two conclusions, the householder's 'give it while you have it' and the renouncer's 'never take it up', and the fragment chooses the more radical one.

gains.a: the householder's alternative, against which its refusal is seen as a choice
gains.b: the renouncer's conclusion from its own premise

links.note: Kural 247 takes as plain fact that this world is not for those without wealth; verse 35 grants that without wealth there is no living but adds that with it base men kill, and that it fails both this world and the next.
links.teaches: The fragment accepts the Kural's premise and then denies it its consolation: wealth is needed for life and still ruins it, so neither world is secured by it.

gains.a: the Kural's plain premise, which it grants before turning it
gains.b: the dangers of possession that its blunt premise about poverty leaves out

links.note: Both have grey hair as the sign and the staff as age's companion; Naladiyar 11 says the wise renounced in infancy foreseeing grey, verse 36's speaker resolves only after forty, when grey has come.
links.teaches: The two measure renunciation by when it comes: the quatrain prizes foresight in childhood, while the fragment shows the ordinary case, a man who turns only when desire has already left him.

gains.a: a standard by which its late resolve is the lesser kind
gains.b: a first-person case of the man its wise contrast pass over, showing what makes him turn at last

links.note: Naladiyar 183 bids one sow seed for the next life without confusion; verse 37 makes it a farmer's whole round, ploughing, sowing and watering, always and always.
links.teaches: Seed for the next life is not one act of sowing but a continuing labour, and the fragment spells out the farming year the quatrain compresses into a word.

gains.a: the explicit term மறுமைக்கு வித்து that names what its farmer is sowing
gains.b: the full labour of the field, which turns its single command into a discipline

links.note: Verse 38 repeats Kural 345 nearly word for word and adds two lines: while the body and ties remain, clinging karma drives the soul through many wombs.
links.teaches: The couplet's paradox, that even the body is too much for one who would end birth, gets its reason in the fragment: the body is where karma takes hold.

gains.a: the authority of the Kural's own words for its opening
gains.b: an account of why the body is excess, which the couplet asserts without explaining

links.note: Kural 350 commands clinging to the one without clinging in order to let clinging go; verse 39 says removing sin while still in attachment is washing blood with blood.
links.teaches: If the Kural's holding to the attachment-free one is itself an attachment, the fragment's simile denies that any attachment can cure another, so a release by devotion and a release by pure letting-go part here; the conflict depends on reading the Kural's பற்று as a real attachment.

gains.a: a rival remedy, devotion as the cure of attachment, against which its blood-washing simile becomes a claim
gains.b: a sharp objection that its 'ladder' of attachment must meet

links.note: Verse 37 holds up the farmer who ploughs, sows and waters as the model of provision; verse 42 shows the ploughman who toils without seed as the fool.
links.teaches: The farmer's image cuts both ways in the fragment: what matters is not the labour, which both farmers do, but whether the seed of austerity was sown.

links.note: Verse 20 bids those who have wealth and pleasure (பொருளடு போகம்) still do austerity; verse 42 says that without austerity the pursuit of wealth and pleasures (பொருளடு போகங்கள்) is fruitless toil.
links.teaches: The pair make austerity both the duty of the prosperous and the cause of prosperity itself, so wealth and pleasure never stand apart from it.

links.note: Kural 377 says even hoarders of millions enjoy only as the apportioner apportioned; verse 42 says that without the seed of austerity the toil for wealth and pleasure bears nothing.
links.teaches: Both deny that effort alone secures enjoyment, but the Kural names an apportioning agent while the fragment puts the cause in one's own past austerity, a karma without a giver.

gains.a: the point that its seed is a form of apportioning, set against a rival account of who apportions
gains.b: a cause without a personal agent, which makes its வகுத்தான் visible as a choice

links.note: In Akananuru 151 the woman reports the man's reason that the poor cannot support dependents or laugh among kin, and says his heart has set grace aside; verse 44 gives the same reason, feeding kin's hunger, as one no one could fault.
links.teaches: The argument for leaving to earn wealth is the same in both, but the akam poem lets the one left behind weigh it against grace, while the fragment's voice treats it as needing no answer.

gains.a: the cost of its argument, borne by the woman left behind
gains.b: a direct statement of the man's case (learning, kin's hunger, the hard road) that the poem gives only as reported speech

links.note: Verse 44 makes feeding hungry kin the reason to seek wealth; verse 45 shows the kin scorning and avoiding a man once he is ruined.
links.teaches: The kin's claim on a man's wealth is not matched by any claim of his on them: their loyalty lasts only as long as the wealth they are owed.

links.note: Kural 796 finds one benefit in ruin, that it measures one's kin; verse 45 shows that measure taken, the kin speaking as they please and standing out of reach.
links.teaches: The Kural turns desertion into knowledge for later choices, while the fragment gives the desertion without consolation, so the 'benefit' appears as what it costs.

gains.a: a frame that makes its bitter scene useful knowledge
gains.b: the concrete scene of desertion that its 'measuring rod' implies

links.note: Verse 4 says women's hearts melt for another as fish delight in new floodwater; verse 46 says a divided woman's mind can no more be made one than oil spread on water gathered.
links.teaches: The fragment moves from women's hearts straying to their being past recall once divided, which completes its case for giving them up.

source_issues: 24 line 2: யஎன்(று) ... சுடுப is probably corrupt; the verse reworks Kuruntokai 17 (பூவென ... எருக்கங் கண்ணியும் சூடுப), so பூஎன்று and சூடுப ('wear') are likely the true readings for யஎன்று and சுடுப ('burn').
29 line 3 and 42 line 3: the checker flags பொய்யடு and பொருளடு as possibly -யொடு/-ளொடு with the vowel sign lost; the sense ('with') supports -ொடு in both, as in verse 20's பொருளடு.
42 line 3 begins யுய்த்தவம், with an initial யு that cannot begin a Tamil word; it looks like a broken sandhi from the line before (உய்த்தவம்).
32 lines 1 and 4 (ஒழிந்த பிறவறன் உண்டென்பார் உட்க; கல்லாப் பிலரே) do not yield a sure sense and may be corrupt.
41 lines 1-2 are obscure; the verse may be the second half of a comparison of the என்னொக்கும் ... ஆறே type (as 39, 42, 46) whose first half is lost or garbled.
47 line 2 (மாண்வினைப் பாவை மறைநின்று கேட்குறிற்) does not fit a clear syntax.
